summary: This work demonstrates measurement-based blind quantum computation on a modular superconducting processor with separate server and client modules, where the server generates two-dimensional cluster states and the client performs universal quantum computation through adaptive measurements without revealing the algorithm or results. The protocol is validated through resource-state characterization, single- and two-qubit gate implementations achieving process fidelities of 0.902 and 0.845, and a three-qubit Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm with 79.7% success probability, with Holevo information of $2.3 \times 10^{-4}$ bits confirming information-theoretic blindness.
motivation: Cloud-based quantum processors lack privacy guarantees for users' algorithms and data. Measurement-based blind quantum computation protocols provide information-theoretic security by enabling clients to delegate computations while hiding both the task and results from the server.
method: A modular superconducting device with three transmon qubits each on server and client modules, flip-chip bonded with inter-module couplers, implements iterative generation of $w \times d$ cluster states at the server and adaptive measurements at the client using real-time feedforward control with a $300$ ns signal processing delay.
result: Two-dimensional cluster states up to $n = 3 \times 3 = 9$ qubits achieved fidelities $F \approx 0.53$; measurement-based T-gate and two-qubit entangling operations reached process fidelities $F_{\mathrm{proc}} = 0.902$ and $0.845$; Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm for $m=2$ inputs succeeded with probability $0.797$; projections with state-of-the-art error rates predict $F > 0.99$ for single-qubit gates and $> 0.98$ for the algorithm.
